previousBinPage.section: Growing Techniques · Making and using compost
previousBinPage.title: A good bin
previousBinPage.subtitle: makes the job easier
previousBinPage.lead: Composting keeps useful material in the garden. Last year’s plant waste becomes part of next year’s growing medium. The important bit is giving it somewhere convenient to break down.
previousBinPage.imageAlt: Three adjoining brick compost bays: an open filling bay, a closed resting bay and an open bay of mature compost.

stages.title: Filling
stages.text: Add new material here as it arrives.

stages.title: Rotting
stages.text: Leave the full bin to break down.

blocks.title: Why three bins help
blocks.text: With two bins, you may need to bag up finished compost to make room. Three bins let each job have its own space. You do not have to shovel the contents along a row: the bins change jobs as they become empty. With only two, finish using one before you need to start filling it again.

blocks.title: Buy one or make one
blocks.text: For a bought bin, look for a sound lid, sturdy sides, a secure rodent-resistant base and an opening you can actually empty through. Check the capacity against your busiest season. A second matching bin is often more useful than a clever gadget attached to the first.

steps.title: Set out the bays
steps.text: Choose a level, accessible spot near both kitchen and garden. Leave working room in front. Fix sound posts securely and use stout boards for the backs, sides and divisions.

steps.title: Make it accessible
steps.text: Use removable front boards so a fork or shovel can reach the bottom. Fit rainproof lids that you can lift safely. Keep some ventilation without leaving the contents exposed on every side.

steps.title: Close the gaps
steps.text: Secure a suitable metal rodent barrier across the base and its edges, while allowing drainage and soil life access. Check joints, lids and damaged boards regularly. Brick walls are an option for a permanent version.
